about.title: San Mateo Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: San Mateo sits at the center of a busy Peninsula health network, with patients traveling along US-101, El Camino Real, and SR-92 to reach hospitals, specialists, and outpatient centers across San Mateo County. Most of that care is careful and competent. Some of it is not, and the difference matters a great deal under California law. A poor result on its own is not malpractice; what has to be shown is that a provider fell below the accepted standard of care and that the lapse caused real harm. That is why a qualified medical expert is almost always part of the case. Timing is tight, too. California's MICRA rules generally give one year from the date the injury was, or should have been, discovered, and never more than three years from the injury itself, with a 90-day notice required before suit is filed. We handle medical malpractice claims in San Mateo and can review your records to explain your options.

items.question: I had a bad outcome at a hospital in San Mateo. Does that mean I have a malpractice case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law is clear that a disappointing or even tragic result, by itself, is not malpractice. What matters is whether a provider departed from the accepted standard of care and whether that departure caused your injury. We will usually need to have the records reviewed by a qualified medical expert before answering that question.

items.question: How much time do I have to act under California's MICRA rules?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from the date you discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury, and in no event more than three years from the date of the injury itself. You must also give the provider 90 days' written notice before filing suit. Because these deadlines can overlap in confusing ways, it helps to speak with us sooner rather than later.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover in a San Mateo County malpractice claim?
items.answer: California places a statutory cap on non-economic damages, such as pain and suffering, in medical malpractice cases, and that cap rises each year under current law. Economic losses like medical bills and lost income are treated separately. We can explain how the cap applies to the facts of your situation without predicting any particular result.
